final_message:
Subject: Week one in the garden

Dear Marcus,

You asked how the garden is getting on, and I am happy to report that it is getting on a good deal better than I am. The first week of planting is over, my back has filed a formal complaint, and I am assured by everyone who knows anything that this is the natural order of things.

On Monday I turned the soil. It had been lying idle since autumn, and it received the spade with the sullen air of a man waked up too early. There were stones in it enough to build a modest chapel. I took out a wheelbarrow-full, and then discovered that the ground had a great many more, which it had been keeping in reserve. Polly looked on from the porch and offered several suggestions, none of them involving her coming down.

Tuesday I put in the peas, along a string stretched between two stakes, because I am told a straight row is the mark of a serious man. Mine bends a little toward the east, as if inclined to see what the neighbors are doing. On Wednesday came the lettuce and the radishes, which are the most obliging of vegetables: they ask little, promise much, and are up almost before you have turned your back. I sowed them thick, and shall be sorry for it when I come to thin them.

The beans and the corn I have held back. The almanac says wait, the old man next door says wait, and the sky, which was soft and blue on Thursday and spiteful on Friday, says wait with some emphasis. A late frost would make a very poor return on an investment of that size. I put in the potatoes, however, on the principle that they are underground and cannot be insulted by the weather.

I should add that the birds have already taken an interest. One robin in particular sits on the fence-post and watches me sow, with the air of an inspector who has not yet decided to approve the work. I have thought of a scarecrow, but I am not sure I could find a coat I would willingly give up.

Do come and see it when the first green shows. I will promise you nothing in the way of a harvest, but there will be lemonade, and a chair in the shade, and I shall not ask you to hold a hoe unless you volunteer.

Yours in mud and good hope,
[name]
